blocks.x: The Race for Hydrogen Fuel Has Taken These Scientists to the Arctic Seafloor. But Can They Unlock Its Secrets Before It’s Too Late?
On challenging expeditions, researchers have collected deep-sea bacteria that naturally produce hydrogen, exploring and documenting an ancient ecosystem that may soon be altered forever

The sun never sets during the Arctic summer; it only flirts with the horizon to create an eerie twilight. From the deck of a research vessel on the seemingly endless expanse of gray, cold ocean, this offers the only natural sense for the passage of days.

Juan Galarza, a molecular ecologist at the University of Oulu in Finland, often lost track of time due to these “disorienting” conditions, as he and his team combed the high Arctic during the summer of 2024. They spent the perpetual daylight obsessively staring at a deep-sea scanner’s monitor and hoping for signs of methane bubbles.

Such a signal could indicate that they had found a cold seep, a deep-sea site from which fluids or gases, like methane, escape through cracks on the seafloor. Through an energy-producing process known as chemosynthesis, microscopic life can sustain itself on these gases, thriving in the total darkness and near-freezing conditions. And some of these bacteria, Galarza believes, could kickstart clean energy innovation.
“These microbes have evolved millions of years there in isolation,” Galarza explains. “This is one of the least explored systems ever.”
Did you know? Cold seeps vs. hydrothermal vents
Both cold seeps and hydrothermal vents lie in deep-sea ecosystems where sunlight doesn’t reach, and they support chemosynthetic organisms that make energy through chemical reactions.

Cold seeps, where fluids and gases like methane and hydrogen sulfide emerge from the seafloor, are typically the temperature of the surrounding water. Hydrothermal vents are hot and linked to volcanism—mineral-rich water, heated by magma to more than 750 degrees Fahrenheit, emerges in these zones.

A fellow marine biologist had alerted Galarza about simple bacteria thought to feed off methane at cold seeps in the Arctic and naturally produce hydrogen as a byproduct of their metabolic cycle. This potential inspired him to dream: If only he could find these microbes in the sediment and study how they produce hydrogen, it could lead to new ways of making hydrogen fuel, a potentially clean and renewable energy source that produces only water as a byproduct when burned.

His team has returned to the Arctic seafloor two times since to find and collect bacteria samples, most recently this summer. Galarza says he’s encouraged by their progress toward harnessing the microbes’ hydrogen-producing genes in sustainable fuel development.

But the Arctic Ocean is undergoing rapid alterations due to climate change. As they search the seafloor for new discoveries, scientists are acutely aware that the life there might change—or even disappear—before it is fully understood.

“We’re studying an ecosystem changing very quickly,” says Henry Huntington, the head of Arctic science research at the Ocean Conservancy, who is not involved with Galarza’s team. “It’s very hard to know which direction things will go.”
The new prospectors

Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe—present in an estimated 90 percent of atoms—but to be used as fuel, it must be harnessed in its pure, unbonded form. Natural hydrogen, as this is known, is rare; to produce it, the element usually needs to be separated from hydrogen-containing molecules, such as water or natural gas.

While hydrogen has the potential to be a clean alternative fuel for combustion engines, the need to isolate the element has prevented it from breaking into mainstream use. Separating hydrogen is an energy-intensive and expensive process, and hydrogen is only a clean energy source if that separation is powered by a renewable grid, rather than by fossil fuels.
But today, demand for alternative energies has resurrected interest in hydrogen fuel, and some industry experts believe it could yet play a crucial role in the energy infrastructure of tomorrow.

“Anywhere that you can use natural gas, you could use hydrogen,” explains Naomi Boness, a geophysicist who previously worked at Chevron but is now the managing director of the Center for Fuels of the Future at Stanford University, which explores methods of decarbonizing key sectors of the global economy.

She sees hydrogen fuel as being particularly useful in heavy industries that would otherwise be difficult to electrify, like aviation or shipping. Cars can go electric, but “it’s really hard to imagine, for example, how you would electrify a long-haul airplane,” Boness says. She estimates that 50 percent of the global economy will still be dependent on combustion engines by 2060. “What are we going to do about all these really fuel-dependent sectors?"

Hydrogen is a potential answer, she says. If breakthroughs make harvesting natural hydrogen more economically and environmentally viable, it could be an “ultimate game changer for humanity,” Boness adds. “It would completely revolutionize how we use energy in our systems.”

Investors and governments are pouring billions into startups and research efforts, hoping to lower the cost and emissions needed to create hydrogen fuel—and by doing so, take hold of a multibillion-dollar industry. Others are betting big on discovering natural hydrogen underground, thereby removing the need to separate it from another molecule.
“It’s like the early days of oil and gas exploration,” Boness says.

blocks.x: For their part, Galarza’s Arctic team—funded by H2Future, a coalition of European governments and energy investors seeking breakthroughs in hydrogen fuel—is exploring the hydrogen-producing bacteria at cold seeps. They plan to study the organisms’ genetics to learn exactly how they produce the gas in near-freezing conditions.

That genetic coding, Galarza says, could inform new hydrogen-related biotechnologies. For example, he could “copy-paste” hydrogen-making enzymes into other bacteria, such as E. coli, that are commonly cultivated at industrial scales in labs. Unlike the cold seep bacteria, E. coli do not require methane to survive, removing the potent greenhouse gas from the production process.

But Galarza says E. coli, spliced with the hydrogen-producing enzymes, offers an advantage over that: The bacteria could be fed industrial waste to grow, helping recycle the refuse from businesses like paper mills. Then, the microbes generate hydrogen, possibly producing higher yields than algae, and could be harvested for fuel and other commercial purposes.

“They are very specialized organisms that have to adapt to these extreme conditions,” Galarza explains. Evolution has made them more simple over time. “They only kept the essential genes and enzymes to survive there, and anything else is gone.”

Any subtle shifts to the biochemistry of the water could force them to adapt to survive—and perhaps lose that “specialist” ability to produce hydrogen.
Today, the Arctic is changing faster than any other region on the planet—and those effects are trickling down to the seafloor.

The loss of sea ice could affect nutrient levels throughout the water column. When spring arrives and sunlight breaks the long Arctic night, life blooms underneath the ice—a garden of algae nourishes creatures at all depths of the ocean.

blocks.x: Changes to salinity also pose significant uncertainties. As waters warm, sea ice retreats and glaciers melt, saltier Atlantic currents have crept further north, a process known as the “Atlantification” of the Arctic. These changes mix the various layers of the Arctic Ocean: Saltier water sinks lower and pushes fresher water to the top, altering the spread of nutrients.

“Biologists still don’t know what would be the response of the ecological system to this new physical environment of layers,” explains Igor Polyakov, an Arctic researcher at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.

Galarza has been startled by the rapid biochemical changes that he’s seen in the water, due to shifting salinity levels and shrinking sea ice that alters the intensity and timing of sunlight breaking through the surface. His team has found more than 800 species of undescribed microbes living near the cold seeps, but many of them could perish due to the changing conditions.
“We are documenting environments that might not be there in ten years,” he says. “We are losing a lot of species there, and I’m just looking at the bacteria.”

Galarza’s team has collected genetic samples from the bacteria and is now working on isolating the hydrogen-producing enzymes. Due to the simplicity of their genetics, this has been easier than Galarza expected.

“I have never been so fast in assembling a genome,” he says. Though there are many steps yet to be completed—such as developing new technologies to capture the hydrogen from the bacteria—he is encouraged by the early results.

While Galarza hopes he has what he needs to continue his hydrogen research, he fears that many of the other microbes living on the Arctic seafloor could disappear before they are studied—and with them, potential secrets to vaccines and cancer treatments or breakthroughs in how we search for extraterrestrial life could also vanish.
“What could be discovered from those environments?” Galarza says. “The potential is unquantifiable.”
